low_extreme_questions.question: A new gene-editing technology could permanently eliminate a serious inherited disease before birth by modifying human embryos. Early evidence suggests the treatment is effective, but scientists remain uncertain about possible unintended genetic consequences that could affect future generations. Some researchers argue that preventing avoidable suffering justifies carefully regulated use of the technology, while others believe altering the human germline crosses an ethical boundary regardless of potential benefits. Regulators must determine whether clinical use should be permitted.

Military satellites have become essential for communication, navigation, intelligence gathering, and national defense. During an international crisis, one country considers disabling another country’s satellites before open conflict begins, believing this would reduce casualties by weakening its opponent’s military capabilities. Critics argue that attacks on space infrastructure could escalate conflict, harm civilians around the world, and undermine the peaceful use of outer space. Leaders must decide whether such actions can ever be ethically justified.

Rapid advances in artificial intelligence and other computational technologies require increasingly large data centers that consume substantial amounts of electricity and freshwater. Supporters argue that these technologies improve productivity, accelerate scientific research, and may ultimately reduce environmental impacts in other industries. Critics counter that expanding computational infrastructure places growing strain on limited natural resources and contributes to long-term environmental degradation. Technology companies must decide how aggressively to continue expanding these systems while balancing innovation against their environmental footprint.

A country permits physician-assisted death for adults experiencing severe and irreversible physical suffering. Lawmakers are now considering extending eligibility to individuals whose suffering results solely from severe, treatment-resistant mental illness. Supporters argue that psychological suffering can be just as profound as physical suffering and that competent adults should retain authority over deeply personal end-of-life decisions. Opponents question whether severe mental illness can impair judgment in ways that make genuine informed consent impossible and worry that expanding eligibility could place vulnerable individuals at greater risk.

Artificial intelligence systems have become capable of diagnosing certain diseases as accurately—or more accurately—than experienced physicians in controlled testing. Some hospitals propose allowing AI systems to make routine diagnostic decisions independently, with physicians reviewing only unusual or disputed cases. Supporters argue that this approach would reduce costs, improve consistency, and expand access to care. Critics worry that removing physicians from routine decisions could erode professional judgment, reduce accountability, and overlook uniquely human aspects of medical care.

high_extreme_questions.question: A team of researchers discovers a previously unnoticed error in one of their influential studies after its findings have already shaped public policy and inspired years of additional research. Correcting the error would likely reduce public confidence in science and call numerous related studies into question, even though the central conclusions remain largely unchanged. Delaying publication of the correction would allow researchers time to verify the full impact of the mistake but would knowingly leave inaccurate information in the scientific record.

You are asked to anonymously review a research paper for publication. After accepting the assignment, you realize the work was almost certainly written by a close professional collaborator whose research you deeply respect. You believe you can evaluate the paper fairly, but you also recognize that your positive opinion of the author’s past work may unconsciously influence your judgment. Declining the review would delay publication and burden the journal with finding another qualified reviewer. You must decide whether to continue reviewing the paper or disclose the potential conflict of interest.

Several years ago, a close friend provided extraordinary emotional support during one of the most difficult periods of your life. Over time, however, you have come to realize that the two of you hold increasingly incompatible moral, political, and social values. Conversations frequently become uncomfortable, and maintaining the friendship has begun to feel emotionally draining. Ending the friendship now feels ungrateful given everything they once did for you, but continuing it feels increasingly dishonest to both of you.

You are serving on a hiring committee for a position on your team. One applicant is a former colleague whom you know to be highly competent, reliable, and pleasant to work with. The rest of the committee has no personal connection to any candidate. You believe your prior experience gives you useful information that interviews cannot capture, but you also worry that your enthusiasm could unfairly influence the committee’s decision. You must decide how much weight, if any, your personal experience should receive during the hiring process.

A former employee asks you to serve as a professional reference while applying for a job they are excited about. During their time working with you, they were dependable and well-liked but consistently struggled with one important aspect of the job that is directly relevant to the new position. Providing a completely positive reference may help them secure an opportunity that could improve their life, while disclosing your concerns could significantly reduce their chances of being hired. You must decide what information you have an ethical obligation to share.

low_extreme_questions.question: A successful author believes that publishing future novels under a pen name associated with a different gender would substantially increase readership among audiences who are currently underrepresented in their genre. The books would accurately represent the experiences of the characters, and no false personal history would be publicly claimed beyond the pseudonym itself. Supporters argue that pen names have long been accepted in literature, while critics contend that adopting an identity associated with a historically underrepresented group for commercial advantage may mislead readers and occupy space intended to amplify marginalized voices.

A large music streaming platform offers artists a program that substantially increases the likelihood their songs will appear in personalized recommendations if they agree to accept significantly lower royalty payments. Listeners are never informed that these recommendations have been influenced by financial agreements rather than solely by the platform’s recommendation algorithm. Smaller artists argue that refusing the program effectively makes their work invisible, while critics contend that the system quietly manipulates consumers and rewards those willing to sacrifice fair compensation for greater exposure.

A professional screenwriter has begun using generative AI to help brainstorm dialogue, suggest plot developments, and overcome writer’s block. Although every screenplay is heavily revised by the writer before publication, AI-generated suggestions occasionally remain in the final work. Producers view the technology as no different from any other creative tool, while some fellow writers argue that relying on AI undermines artistic authenticity and threatens opportunities for human creators. The writer must decide how, if at all, AI should be incorporated into their creative process.

Artificial intelligence systems have become capable of diagnosing certain diseases as accurately—or more accurately—than experienced physicians in controlled testing. Some hospitals propose allowing AI systems to make routine diagnostic decisions independently, with physicians reviewing only unusual or disputed cases. Supporters argue that this approach would reduce costs, improve consistency, and expand access to care. Critics worry that removing physicians from routine decisions could erode professional judgment, reduce accountability, and overlook uniquely human aspects of medical care.

A startup has created an artificial intelligence system capable of detecting certain rare diseases significantly earlier than existing methods. Internal testing suggests the system performs exceptionally well overall but occasionally produces extremely confident false negatives in patient populations that were underrepresented during development. Delaying release by another year would allow those weaknesses to be substantially reduced, but thousands of patients who could benefit immediately would continue receiving slower, less accurate diagnoses.

high_extreme_questions.question: Following a devastating terrorist attack, intelligence agencies identify a location where they believe the leaders of the terrorist organization are hiding. The information is credible but uncertain, and civilians are likely to be present. Waiting for better intelligence increases the risk of future attacks, while acting immediately may cause civilian casualties and inflame regional tensions. Decision-makers must determine what level of uncertainty and collateral risk is ethically acceptable when responding to terrorism.

A government employee is instructed to participate in implementing a policy they sincerely believe is seriously unethical, though the policy remains entirely legal under current law. Refusing the assignment will likely end their career and prevent them from influencing future decisions from within the organization. Remaining in the position may allow them to quietly reduce some of the policy’s harmful effects, but it also requires actively contributing to actions they believe are morally wrong. The employee must decide whether ethical responsibility is better served through principled refusal or continued participation.

During a severe public health emergency, a hospital has enough specialized staff to operate only one of two critical treatment units at full capacity. One unit primarily serves patients with acute, life-threatening illnesses, while the other provides ongoing treatment that prevents serious long-term complications for a much larger group of patients. Physicians disagree about whether ethical obligations require prioritizing those facing immediate danger or maximizing the overall health of the broader population. Hospital leadership must decide how to allocate its limited personnel.

Several countries recognize that solving a global problem—such as climate change, pandemic preparedness, or artificial intelligence governance—requires coordinated international action. Each country would benefit if everyone cooperated, but acting first would impose immediate economic or political costs that competitors might avoid. Leaders must determine whether governments have ethical obligations to accept short-term national disadvantages in order to improve long-term outcomes for the international community.

While walking home, you discover a wallet containing a large amount of cash along with identification belonging to someone who appears to be financially secure. Later that evening, you learn through a community organization that a family in your neighborhood urgently needs nearly the same amount of money to avoid eviction and has exhausted all available assistance. Returning the wallet would restore someone’s rightful property, while using the money to help the family could dramatically improve several lives. There is virtually no chance your actions would ever be discovered. You must decide what ethical obligations arise from finding another person’s property.

low_extreme_questions.question: University administrators receive multiple independent reports suggesting that several members of a highly successful athletic program have engaged in serious misconduct toward other students. The available evidence is concerning but incomplete, and publicly acknowledging the allegations before investigations conclude may irreparably damage the reputations of innocent individuals as well as the institution itself. Delaying action, however, may expose additional students to harm if the allegations ultimately prove accurate. Administrators must determine how to respond while balancing fairness, transparency, and campus safety.

A multinational technology company discovers that several overseas suppliers maintain working conditions that fall well below the standards expected in the company’s home country. The suppliers are operating legally under local regulations, and immediately ending the contracts would likely eliminate thousands of jobs in communities that depend heavily on those factories. Continuing the relationship without significant changes may expose workers to unacceptable conditions, while demanding rapid reforms could increase costs enough to make the suppliers financially unsustainable. Company leadership must determine how to respond.

A coastal community depends almost entirely on commercial fishing for its livelihood. Marine scientists recommend closing a large section of nearby waters for at least ten years to allow several collapsing fish populations to recover. If implemented, the policy would likely preserve the ecosystem for future generations but would immediately threaten the economic survival of many local families and businesses. Continuing current fishing practices may sustain the community in the short term while increasing the risk of permanent ecological collapse.

A college athlete discovers that a longtime teammate unknowingly violated an eligibility rule because of incorrect advice provided by the university. Reporting the violation would likely remove the team from championship contention and end the teammate’s collegiate career, despite the lack of intentional wrongdoing. Remaining silent would almost certainly allow the violation to go undiscovered, but the team’s achievements would technically rest on an ineligible participant.

low_extreme_questions.conflict: Humanitarian Responsibility vs Rule of Law
low_extreme_questions.question: A country experiences a large increase in children arriving at its borders without parents or legal guardians. Many appear to be fleeing dangerous conditions, while others may have been encouraged to migrate by relatives already living in the country. Resources for housing, healthcare, and legal processing are limited, and officials disagree about how the government should balance humanitarian obligations toward vulnerable children with the responsibility to enforce immigration laws consistently. Policies adopted now are also expected to influence future migration patterns.

high_extreme_questions.question: A government proposes allowing incarcerated individuals to voluntarily donate a kidney or bone marrow in exchange for a meaningful reduction in their prison sentence. Supporters argue that the program could save lives, reduce shortages of transplantable organs, and provide incarcerated individuals with an opportunity to make a meaningful contribution to society. Critics argue that the offer of earlier freedom creates unavoidable coercion, making genuine consent impossible within a prison environment. Others contend that denying incarcerated people the opportunity to make this choice unfairly strips them of their autonomy simply because they are imprisoned.

Your sibling was recently convicted of a nonviolent financial crime. Although they have accepted responsibility and are attempting to rebuild their life, finding employment has become nearly impossible because of their criminal record. They ask you to use your professional reputation and personal connections to recommend them for a position without volunteering information about their conviction unless specifically asked. Some members of your family argue that helping them move forward is the compassionate thing to do. Others believe doing so would unfairly expose employers to risks they deserve to evaluate for themselves.

A country permits physician-assisted death for adults experiencing severe and irreversible physical suffering. Lawmakers are now considering extending eligibility to individuals whose suffering results solely from severe, treatment-resistant mental illness. Supporters argue that psychological suffering can be just as profound as physical suffering and that competent adults should retain authority over deeply personal end-of-life decisions. Opponents question whether severe mental illness can impair judgment in ways that make genuine informed consent impossible and worry that expanding eligibility could place vulnerable individuals at greater risk.

Researchers propose creating a national health database containing anonymized medical records from every citizen to accelerate research on diseases, improve treatment recommendations, and better detect public health threats. Although strict safeguards would be implemented, some citizens object to having their medical information included without explicit consent, arguing that privacy should not be sacrificed for societal benefit. Others contend that widespread participation is ethically justified because everyone stands to benefit from improved healthcare knowledge.

A government is considering requiring every adult citizen to complete one year of national service, with participants able to choose among military service, disaster relief, environmental restoration, education, or healthcare support. Supporters argue that shared service strengthens communities, develops civic responsibility, and addresses critical public needs. Opponents contend that compelling individuals to devote a year of their lives to government-directed service violates personal liberty, regardless of the available options. Lawmakers must decide whether civic obligations can ethically justify mandatory service.

low_extreme_questions.question: Parents with substantial financial resources offer to make a large donation to a public school if administrators agree to implement several requests that would directly benefit their own children, including smaller class sizes and access to specialized academic programs. School officials believe the donation would improve educational opportunities for many students but worry that granting individualized accommodations based on wealth could undermine principles of equal treatment and public trust. The parents argue that they are simply using their resources to do what any responsible parent would do.

A parent with significant financial resources learns of a legal program that, while technically permitted under current regulations, allows wealthy families to substantially increase their children’s chances of admission to highly competitive universities through exclusive access to specialized opportunities unavailable to most applicants. Using the program would not involve fraud or deception, but many educators argue that it reinforces existing inequalities and undermines confidence in the fairness of admissions. The parent must decide whether pursuing every available advantage for their child is ethically justified.

An employee working for a large advertising agency is assigned to lead a campaign promoting a product they personally believe contributes to serious social harm, despite being entirely legal. Refusing the assignment would likely harm their career and place additional burdens on coworkers, while accepting it would require publicly supporting a message that conflicts with their deeply held moral convictions. The employer argues that personal beliefs should remain separate from professional responsibilities, while the employee believes ethical integrity should extend to their work.

A successful retail company has built its reputation on paying employees well above the industry average while providing generous benefits and opportunities for advancement. During an economic downturn, investors pressure executives to reduce labor costs in order to maximize short-term profits and remain competitive with rivals who pay substantially lower wages. Company leaders believe maintaining current compensation will strengthen the business over the long term but recognize that doing so may disappoint investors and reduce future expansion opportunities.

low_extreme_questions.conflict: Preventive Security vs Justified Use of Force
low_extreme_questions.question: Two neighboring countries have long been rivals. One begins constructing large military installations near the shared border but has not threatened or attacked its neighbor. Intelligence agencies disagree about whether the buildup signals preparation for invasion or is purely defensive. Political leaders in the neighboring country are debating whether launching a preventive military strike before an attack occurs would better protect their citizens or instead violate the moral principles governing the use of force.

high_extreme_questions.conflict: Freedom of Expression vs Responsibility to Protect
high_extreme_questions.question: While moderating a large online community, you notice a long post from a member expressing profound hopelessness and suggesting they may not want to continue living. Other members are responding with empathy, but no one knows the person’s real identity or location. Removing the post could reduce harmful discussion but might also silence someone reaching out for help. Leaving it untouched could allow supportive conversations to continue, but it also risks missing an opportunity to intervene if the situation is urgent. As the moderator, what do you believe is the most ethically justified course of action?

You frequently purchase used books, movies, and music because doing so is substantially less expensive and reduces unnecessary waste. A friend argues that consistently buying secondhand deprives authors, musicians, and other creators of income needed to continue producing new work. Others contend that once a product has been legitimately purchased, owners should be free to resell it without creating any additional ethical obligations for future buyers. You begin wondering whether your purchasing habits create responsibilities beyond simply following the law.

You are a mental health professional meeting with a patient who describes increasingly severe thoughts of ending their own life. They are calm, cooperative, and ask you not to involve family members or emergency services, explaining that they sought help specifically because they wanted confidential support. You believe there is some possibility of imminent harm but are uncertain how immediate the risk truly is. Breaking confidentiality could damage the therapeutic relationship and discourage future help-seeking, while maintaining confidentiality could expose the patient to significant danger. What do you believe is the most ethically justified course of action?

One of your closest friends has struggled with severe depression for many years. You have spent considerable time supporting them, often at significant emotional cost to yourself. Recently, you have begun to feel that maintaining the friendship is seriously affecting your own mental health and relationships with others. At the same time, you worry that distancing yourself may leave them feeling abandoned during a period when they are especially vulnerable. Other mutual friends disagree about whether stepping back would be an understandable act of self-care or an unethical failure to support someone in need.

Supporters argue that these technologies improve productivity, accelerate scientific research, and may ultimately reduce environmental impacts in other industries. Critics counter that expanding computational infrastructure places growing strain on limited natural resources and contributes to long-term environmental degradation. Technology companies must decide how aggressively to continue expanding these systems while balancing innovation against their environmental footprint.

low_extreme_questions.question: A casual acquaintance whom you have known for several years has recently begun expressing views that you believe are deeply prejudiced toward certain groups of people. Although these views have never been directed at you personally, they make you uncomfortable, and you have started questioning whether maintaining the relationship indirectly signals acceptance of those beliefs. In the past, you included this person in social gatherings and public photos, and mutual friends continue to associate the two of you. Some people argue that distancing yourself is a moral responsibility, while others believe that abandoning relationships discourages understanding and change.

One partner in a long-term relationship regularly looks through the other’s phone without permission, explaining that complete openness should exist between people who truly trust one another. The other partner believes that maintaining some degree of personal privacy is compatible with a healthy relationship and feels increasingly uncomfortable with the repeated invasions of privacy, despite having nothing significant to hide. Attempts to discuss the issue have led to repeated disagreements about what trust actually requires.

A close friend spent several years writing a memoir about deeply traumatic experiences. Before publishing it, they told you that your opinion matters more than almost anyone else’s and asked you to read the manuscript. You have no objection to the subject matter itself, but you know reading it would be emotionally exhausting and require a significant amount of time that you simply do not have. When you politely decline, your friend tells you that refusing to read the book demonstrates a lack of support not only for them personally but also for others who have experienced similar trauma. They say that friends who truly care should be willing to make sacrifices for one another during important moments.

A hiring manager learns through informal conversations that an exceptionally qualified job applicant previously struggled with substance abuse but has since maintained several years of recovery. The applicant was never required to disclose this history and has done nothing dishonest during the hiring process. Some members of the hiring committee believe the information should influence the hiring decision because the position carries significant responsibility. Others argue that considering information the applicant had no obligation to reveal unfairly punishes successful rehabilitation.

The employer argues that personal beliefs should remain separate from professional responsibilities, while the employee believes ethical integrity should extend to their work.

A hospital has developed an experimental treatment that offers a moderate chance of extending the life of patients with an otherwise terminal illness. The treatment also carries a significant risk of permanently impairing memory and decision-making ability. One patient has clearly stated that maintaining independence is more important than living longer, but after speaking with family members, the medical team suspects the patient does not fully appreciate how much meaningful time the treatment could provide. The treatment must begin within 24 hours or the opportunity will be lost.

A powerful earthquake devastates a large city, leaving emergency responders with far fewer rescue teams than locations requesting assistance. Officials receive credible reports that one collapsed building contains dozens of trapped residents with only a small chance of survival, while another contains far fewer people but a much greater likelihood of successful rescue. Rescue teams cannot reach both locations in time. Leaders must decide whether resources should be directed toward saving the greatest number of lives, helping those in greatest need regardless of probability, or according to some other principle.

A wealthy country has developed an effective vaccine during the early stages of a rapidly spreading global disease. Domestic demand remains high, and political leaders have promised that every citizen who wants the vaccine will receive it before any doses are exported. Public health experts argue that sending a substantial portion of the supply to countries experiencing uncontrolled outbreaks would ultimately save more lives worldwide and reduce the risk of dangerous new variants emerging, but doing so would delay protection for many citizens at home.

A physician works for a healthcare organization that receives additional reimbursement when patient records include extensive documentation of potential health risks and secondary diagnoses. The additional documentation is legal and often medically relevant, but completing it substantially reduces the time physicians can spend speaking directly with patients. Administrators strongly encourage the practice and emphasize the financial benefits it brings to the organization, while physicians receive no additional compensation for the extra work. One physician begins intentionally limiting this documentation in order to prioritize patient care during appointments, despite repeated encouragement from management to maximize reporting.

fold_axis_recovery.interpretation: Each fold tests its own training-defined PCA axes. Because PCA components can swap or rotate across folds, these tests are summarized across the six-dimensional set and are not attached to the post-hoc labels from the all-model descriptive fit.

interpretation_warning: This is a secondary whole-geometry analysis, not topic-controlled. Axes are learned without ethical labels. Descriptive names are assigned afterward from extreme-question annotations and are not independent validation or mapped to fold-specific component numbers.
